1.pericope_label: David sends to comfort Hanun, whose princes suspect espionage; the ambassadors are half shaved and sent home by way of Jericho

schools.summary: Ellicott observes that the kindness David meant to repay is not recorded, and may have been friendly help during the wanderings or merely a congratulatory embassy on his accession; he makes this Nahash probably a son or grandson of the Nahash whom Saul conquered, since more than fifty years must have passed since that event. He allows the Ammonite suspicion some real ground, Rabbah being the capital and almost the only city of the nation, strongly fortified, so that knowledge of its interior would be important to an enemy, while the fear may have been roused by David’s growing power and especially by his conquest of the neighbouring Moabites. He calls the half-shaving the extremest insult Oriental ideas could inflict, and takes the Arab testimony for it expressly from Keil; he adds the remark that in none of David’s wars does he appear as the aggressor. On the halt he notes that Jericho lay directly on their road, and resolves the old curse by philology: the city had been destroyed at the entrance into Canaan with a curse on whoever should build it, which fell upon Hiel more than a century after David, but build here means fortify, and Jericho, under the name of the city of palm trees, appears to have been an inhabited place all along. Keil and Delitzsch open the section by placing this war where the shadow falls across the reign, since it was during the war with the Ammonites and Syrians, while Joab besieged their capital and David remained in Jerusalem, that he stained his soul with adultery and murder, falling the deeper because of the height to which God had exalted him. On the embassy they read the two questions of the princes grammatically, the first framed to expect a negative answer and the second to require an affirmative, and identify the city to be spied as the capital Rabbah. They gather the comparative evidence on the beard, that among the Arabs cutting off a man’s beard is reckoned an indignity quite equal to flogging and branding among ourselves and that many would rather die than suffer it, and they add a modern parallel in which a pretender to the Persian throne, having sent to demand tribute and had his ambassadors’ beards cut off instead, came the next year with a large army. They give their own reason for the halt at Jericho, that David might not have to set his eyes upon the insult his servants had received.

Clarke takes the obligation to have been personal and political at once: we do not know exactly its nature or extent, but this Nahash is likely the same who attacked Jabesh-gilead and whom Saul defeated, and since David had taken refuge with the Moabites next door, Nahash’s hatred of Saul might well have induced him to show the fugitive particular kindness. On the suspicion of the princes he generalises, that it has been a matter of just complaint through all the history of mankind that there is little sincerity in courts, courtiers being suspicious of each other and often misleading their sovereigns, because they feel themselves insincere and suspect others to be so too. On the beard he explains that its possessor counts it his greatest ornament, often swears by it and in matters of great importance pledges it, no pledge being more secure since its owner will redeem it at the hazard of his life; it was never cut off but in mourning or as a sign of slavery, so that halving the beard and the garments together rendered the men ridiculous and made them look like slaves, an accumulation of insult. On Jericho he holds the town unrebuilt since the time of Joshua, its walls unrepaired though many cottages and larger dwellings doubtless remained, and therefore comparatively private, so that the men would not be exposed to public notice. Wesley reads the shaving as fastening a reproach upon them to make them ridiculous and contemptible, and judges the cutting of the garments the worse of the two indignities, because the Israelites wore no breeches and their nakedness was hereby uncovered.

Henry is less interested in the donor of the kindness than in the debt. The inducement was some kindness formerly received from Nahash, and having lately had the satisfaction of showing kindness to Mephibosheth for his father’s sake, David resolves on the same here, for the pleasure of doing one kind and generous action should excite us to another. Nahash had been a cruel enemy to Israel and may have shown kindness only in contradiction to Saul; but if David receives kindness he is not nice in examining the grounds and principles of it, since God knows the heart and we do not. On the embassy itself Henry notes that it is a comfort to children, when their parents are dead, to find that their parents’ friends are theirs. The princes’ suspicion he makes pure projection: false men are ready to think others as false as themselves, and the Ammonites would never have imagined that David dissembled had they not been conscious that they could have dissembled to serve a turn — unfounded suspicion argues a wicked mind, and he borrows from Bishop Patrick that there is nothing so well meant but it may be ill interpreted, and is wont to be so by men who love nobody but themselves. On the affront he is blunt, that Hanun behaved like a man of a sordid villainous spirit, fitter to rake a kennel than to wear a crown, abusing men who were under the special protection of the law of nations and who had come unarmed. On the halt he explains the practical point, that the shaved half must grow until the other could be decently cut to it, the Jews wearing their beards long and reckoning it an honour to appear aged and grave, and that change of raiment they likely had but beards would not be so soon repaired.

Gill sets the chronology, that this followed the wars with the Moabites, Syrians and Edomites, and that the spoils of the children of Ammon mentioned earlier in the book are given by anticipation, since they were not taken until the war now beginning. He identifies the princes as the nobles and prime ministers, the courtiers about the king, and explains that the news reached David before the ambassadors themselves did, some of their servants having been sent ahead to acquaint him with the usage they had met with.

debates.question: Which Nahash had shown kindness to David, and what was the kindness?

positions.view: Probably a son or grandson of the Nahash Saul conquered, more than fifty years having passed; the kindness perhaps help during the wanderings
Likely the same Nahash who attacked Jabesh-gilead, whose hatred of Saul would incline him to befriend the fugitive David
Does not press the question: David received kindness and is not nice in examining the grounds of it

debates.question: Was the Ammonite princes’ suspicion of espionage reasonable?

positions.view: It had real ground: Rabbah was strongly fortified and worth spying on, and David’s power was growing
Pure projection: false men think others as false as themselves, and unfounded suspicion argues a wicked mind
A standing vice of courts, where courtiers feel themselves insincere and suspect others to be so

debates.question: Why Jericho, and was it then an inhabited place?

positions.view: Unrebuilt since Joshua and comparatively private, though cottages and larger dwellings remained
Inhabited all along as the city of palm trees; the curse was on fortifying it, and fell on Hiel a century later
A private place where the men need not come into company until their beards could be evened
Chosen so that David might not have to set his eyes upon the insult his servants had received

outliers.claim: Alone in opening the chapter with the Bathsheba sin for which this war is the setting, and alone in supplying a modern parallel for the beard insult from Persian diplomacy.
Alone in resolving the curse on Jericho by reading build as fortify, and alone in observing that David never appears as the aggressor in any of his wars.
Alone in reading the embassy through the earlier kindness to Mephibosheth, and alone in citing Bishop Patrick on well-meant things ill interpreted.

themes: the king of the children of Ammon died, and Hanun his son reigned in his stead
I will shew kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father shewed kindness unto me
David sent to comfort him by the hand of his servants
thinkest thou that David doth honour thy father, that he hath sent comforters unto thee?
hath not David rather sent his servants unto thee, to search the city, and to spy it out?
Hanun took David’s servants, and shaved off the one half of their beards
cut off their garments in the middle, even to their buttocks
tarry at Jericho until your beards be grown, and then return

6.pericope_label: The Ammonites hire the Syrians, Joab divides his force between the two armies, and both enemies are routed

schools.summary: Ellicott prices the war from the parallel at a thousand talents of silver, variously estimated from a hundred and twenty-five thousand pounds to twice that, which shows at once the wealth of Ammon, the importance of the auxiliaries and the grave character of the struggle; he corrects two names, reading king of Maacah for king Maacah and men of Tob for Ish-tob, the first syllable being no part of the proper name. On Beth-rehob he rejects the identification with the Rehob of Numbers and Judges, since that lay near Laish within Israelite territory, and prefers Rehoboth by the river near the Euphrates as answering to the words out of Mesopotamia in the parallel, though he notes that some would place it at a site twenty-five miles north-east of Damascus. He reports that the allies mustered at Medeba, a hill town well fitted strategically to repel an attack upon Rabbah and originally assigned to Reuben, and presses the numerical discrepancy that the totals agree once Maacah is left out of the reckoning while the composition does not, this text naming only infantry and the parallel only chariots and cavalry, although the result of the battle makes it plain that all three arms were engaged — so that either words have dropped out of both texts or neither writer cared to go into details. On the tactics he credits deliberate design: the keen eye of this experienced general took in both the advantage and the danger at once, and he threw his whole force between the two divisions of the enemy, organising it in two parts each capable of supporting the other, so that the enemy was cut in two while the Israelites formed one compact body, Joab taking the wing facing the Syrians with the choice troops as having the stronger foe. On the speech he renders the opening literally as be strong and let us strengthen ourselves, and mends the close, which should read not that the Lord do what seemeth him good but that he will do it, finding Joab’s courage rising to that highest point marked by full trust that whatever the result it will be what seems best to infinite wisdom and love. Keil and Delitzsch make Beth-rehob the capital of an Aramaean kingdom and in all probability the city of Numbers and Judges south of Hamath, whose exact position has not been discovered; they put the hire at nearly half a million pounds sterling, place the Syrians apart on the broad treeless table-land by Medeba some four geographical miles south-west of Rabbath-Ammon, and defend the text against Thenius, who would insert a conjunction before the mighty men, since no distinction is ever drawn between the heroes and the whole army. On the speech they explain why Joab could call the towns of Israel the towns of our God, the God of Israel having given the land to his people as his own property, so that the brothers fought lest Jehovah’s possessions fall into the hands of the heathen and become subject to their gods.

Clarke glosses the Hebrew idiom that the Ammonites stank before David as meaning that their conduct rendered them abominable, and places the hired contingents, Beth-rehob at the extremity of the valley between Libanus and Anti-libanus, Zoba subject to Hadadezer, Maacah in the vicinity of Mount Hermon beyond Jordan, and Ish-tob probably the Tob in Gilead to which Jephthah fled from the cruelty of his brethren. He identifies the place of battle as Medeba from the parallel, and reconstructs the movement that produced Joab’s predicament: one of the armies was in the field and the other in the city when Joab arrived, so that when he fronted the first the second issued from the city and took him in the rear, obliging him to divide his force, one part under himself to face the Syrians and the other under his brother Abishai to face the Ammonites. Of the speech he says it is a very fine military address, equal to anything in ancient or modern times, the men fighting for hearth and altar, for every good thing sacred and civil, for God and their families and their country.

Henry reads the Ammonite preparations as the folly of a provoked quarrel: they might easily have foreseen their danger when they abused the ambassadors, which was no other than a challenge to war, yet had not considered how unable they were with their thousands to meet David’s, and so were forced to hire the forces of other nations — had they humbled themselves and begged pardon, an honorary satisfaction might probably have atoned for the offence, but being desperately resolved to stand by what they had done they courted their own ruin. He commends David’s prudence in carrying the war into their country, since the terrors and desolations of war are such that a good prince will in love to his people keep it at a distance from them. On the division of the force he supposes Joab kept the choicest men against the Syrians, whom he probably knew to be the better soldiers and, being hired men, better versed in the arts of war, and he grants that Joab’s conduct and courage were never so tried as now, since when he saw the front of the battle against him both before and behind he animated his men to charge the more furiously instead of ordering an honourable retreat. The speech he finds not long but pertinent and brave, drawing from the arrangement between the brothers that mutual helpfulness is brotherly duty, each to relieve the other upon a signal if his part should be borne hard upon; great dangers put an edge upon true courage, and the men were to be valiant not for pay and preferment nor for honour and fame but for their people and the cities of their God.

Gill explains that the Ammonites, instead of seeking to appease a king they knew to be incensed, made themselves more odious still, and leaves the muster open, having them come out either from Rabbah their metropolis, as Josephus says, or rather from Medeba, a frontier town upon their borders. He notes that Joab, having two armies against him before and behind, divided his own into two parts that he might the better attack them, and that he addressed his speech not only to Abishai but in the hearing of the officers and many of the people, who might well be intimidated by the number of their enemies and the position they were in. On the battle he judges that Joab attacked the Syrians first, rightly reckoning that hired soldiers closely pressed would give way, which would discourage the Ammonites who depended so much upon them.

debates.question: Where was Beth-rehob, from which the Syrian mercenaries came?

positions.view: In all probability the city of Numbers and Judges, south of Hamath, its exact position undiscovered
Hardly that one, which lay near Laish inside Israel; more likely Rehoboth by the river, near the Euphrates
At the extremity of the valley between Libanus and Anti-libanus

debates.question: Did Joab divide his force by design or by necessity?

positions.view: By design: he threw his force between the two divisions so the enemy was cut in two and Israel formed one compact body
By necessity: the second army issued from the city and took him in the rear, obliging him to divide
By judgment of quality: the choicest men against the Syrians, the better soldiers and better versed in war

debates.question: How should the closing words of Joab’s speech be read?

positions.view: Not a prayer but a confession: the Lord will do what seemeth him good
A recognition that the towns are God’s own property, lest they fall to the heathen and their gods
A leaving of the issue with God once the men have done their part

outliers.claim: Alone in pressing that the two accounts agree in total but not in composition, so that either both texts have lost words or neither writer cared for details.
Alone in holding that an apology would probably have settled the quarrel, and alone in commending David for keeping the war at a distance from his own people.
Alone in explaining why Joab struck the Syrians first, that hired soldiers closely pressed would give way and dishearten those who depended on them.

the children of Ammon put the battle in array at the entering in of the gate

be of good courage, and let us play the men for our people, and for the cities of our God

15.pericope_label: The Syrians rally beyond the river, David crosses to Helam and routs them, Shobach is slain and the vassal kings make peace

schools.summary: Henry makes the regathering a law of lost causes, since even the baffled cause will make head as long as there is any life in it, and the Syrians, conscious of their insufficiency, called in their allies and dependencies from the other side of the river, hoping to make their part good against Israel — but they knew not the thoughts of the Lord, who gathered them as sheaves into the floor. He commends David’s vigilance in refusing to wait until he was attacked, going in person at the head of his army over Jordan. On the casualties he harmonises the two accounts without remark, reading seven thousand men who belonged to seven hundred chariots together with forty thousand other soldiers, horse and foot. He reads the outcome as the fulfilment of an old promise, the borders of Israel reaching the river Euphrates as was said to Abraham and repeated to Joshua, performed at length; and he presses the reason the allies withdrew, that the Syrians feared to help the children of Ammon any more not because they had an unrighteous cause, though the abuse of ambassadors was a breach of the law of nations, but because they found it an unsuccessful one — for it is dangerous helping those who have God against them, since when they fall their helpers will fall with them.

Ellicott reads the rally from Hadarezer’s side, that he felt the importance of the defeat he had sustained and made an effort to rally all his forces, calling together even vassal tribes from beyond the Euphrates, while David took the field in person and Joab was more probably employed in the south, holding the Ammonites in check and preventing their forming a junction with their confederates. On Helam he is careful: the Hebrew word is not necessarily a proper name and might be rendered their host, but since the name unquestionably occurs in the following verse it is better taken as a name here also; it is omitted altogether from the parallel, and though its exact situation is unknown it plainly lay in the general direction of the Euphrates and not very far from Hamath. On the numbers he decides between the readings, holding seven thousand chariots almost an incredible number and the seven hundred of this text evidently the more correct, while the parallel’s forty thousand footmen against this text’s forty thousand horsemen probably means that both statements are meant to include infantry and cavalry with only one of the two specified in each place; and he judges that in this campaign David delivered a crushing blow from which his foes did not recover during the rest of his reign or that of his son. On the peace he parts from Keil and Delitzsch: it is not said that Hadarezer himself became a tributary, though he was greatly weakened and lost large booty, and since a dependent of his afterwards maintained himself in the territory of Damascus as an enemy of Israel, while Solomon is said to have reigned over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates, it is no more than probable that Hadarezer too acknowledged the suzerainty of David and his son. Keil and Delitzsch read the muster as plainly under Hadarezer’s supreme authority, since his own general commanded the Mesopotamian troops and the kings who fought with him are afterwards called his servants, and they report that Shobach was so smitten that he did not survive the battle. On the peace they take the opposite view, granting that the first half of the verse might suggest only the vassals submitted, but holding that the closing clause, that Aram feared to help the Ammonites any more, shows very clearly that Hadarezer also made peace and became subject, so that the earlier expression is simply not a very exact one.

Clarke identifies the river as the Euphrates and this Hadarezer as the Hadadezer overthrown earlier in the book, which is the reading here of about thirty of the manuscripts collated by Kennicott and De Rossi, the two Hebrew letters concerned being easily interchanged; and he notes that such a war required the king’s own presence. On the numbers he offers a general theory of corruption rather than a decision: in former times the Jews expressed their numbers not by words at full length but by numeral letters, and since many of those letters closely resemble each other, mistakes easily crept in when the letters came to be written out in words — the characters for seven thousand and seven hundred being just such a pair, which alone would account for many of the numerical disagreements found in these books. On the settlement he notes that the vassals made their peace separately and were obliged to pay tribute, and reports a reading found in some copies of the Vulgate and nowhere else, which adds that fifty-eight thousand of them were panic-struck and fled before Israel. He closes the first half of the book with a reckoning: in nineteen or twenty years David had finished eight wars, all righteously undertaken and all honourably terminated, and the promise to Abraham was accomplished — but the splendour of this illustrious epoch is about to be obscured by crimes of which one could never have suspected him capable, so that he who most assuredly standeth should take heed lest he fall. Wesley repeats Henry’s two closing points in brief, that the promise to Abraham and Joshua of a border at the Euphrates was now fulfilled, and that the Son of David sent his apostles and ministers to the Jewish nation as David sent his ambassadors to Hanun, who entreated them shamefully, mocked them and slew them, which filled the measure of their iniquity and brought upon them ruin without remedy.

Gill has the Syrians consider the defeat among themselves and fear what would come of it, identifies Hadarezer with the Hadadezer at the head of the confederacy to whom the rest of the kings of Syria were servants, and notes that the Syrians fled only after an obstinate and bloody fight. Of the vassals he observes that they had been subject to Hadarezer, at his beck and command, or at least hired by him into his service.

debates.question: How are the casualty figures of the two accounts to be handled?

positions.view: By textual explanation: numbers were once written as numeral letters, and those for seven hundred and seven thousand are easily confused
By decision: seven thousand chariots is almost incredible, so seven hundred is the more correct reading
By harmonising: seven thousand men belonging to seven hundred chariots, besides forty thousand horse and foot

debates.question: Did Hadarezer himself submit to David, or only his vassal kings?

positions.view: He submitted too; the closing clause about Aram’s fear shows it clearly, the first half of the verse being inexact
It is not said that he became a tributary; a dependent of his later held Damascus against Israel, so his submission is only probable
The vassals made peace separately and were obliged to pay tribute

debates.question: Is Helam a place name at all?

positions.view: The word need not be a name and might be rendered their host, but the next verse settles it as a name; its site is unknown
Treats it as the place where the Aramaeans set themselves in array and were smitten

debates.question: Why did the Syrians stop helping Ammon?

positions.view: Not because the cause was unrighteous but because it had proved unsuccessful; it is dangerous to help those who have God against them
Because the blow was crushing, and they did not recover during the rest of David’s reign or his son’s

outliers.claim: Alone in reporting the Vulgate addition of fifty-eight thousand panic-struck fugitives, a reading nowhere else to be found, and alone in closing with a tally of David’s eight wars.
Alone in questioning whether Helam is a proper name, and alone in denying from 1 Kings that Hadarezer himself became tributary.
